overview:
Samādhitantram (समाधितन्त्रम्), often rendered in English as “Supreme Meditation” or “Attainment of Oneness with the Supreme Self,” is a concise but highly influential Jain Sanskrit treatise traditionally attributed to Ācārya Pūjyapāda, a major Digambara ācārya of roughly the 5th century CE. The work consists of around 105 metrical verses and belongs to the genre of upadeśa (instructional) texts that outline the inner path of liberation rather than external ritual. It is studied across Digambara circles as a systematic guide to understanding the nature of the soul (jīva), its entanglement in karmic bondage, and the meditative discipline required to realize the pure soul (paramātmā).

The opening maṅgalācaraṇa (invocatory verse) situates the text firmly within the Jain spiritual universe by bowing to Lord Mahāvīra as Tīrthaṅkara and ford-maker, the one who illuminates the flawless awakened self and shows the path of liberation. From the outset, Samādhitantram announces its central concern: immersion (samādhi) in the supreme self, not as a vague mystical state but as a precise, doctrinally grounded realization of the soul’s true nature free from all karmic impurities. The text thus integrates devotion to the Jina with rigorous philosophical discrimination between soul and non-soul.

A distinctive doctrinal framework in Samādhitantram is its description of three modes or standpoints of the soul: the extroverted-soul (bahirātmā), the introverted-soul (antarātmā), and the pure-soul (paramātmā). The bahirātmā is the deluded standpoint that identifies the body, senses, and external possessions as the self; such a person spends life in confusion and suffering. The antarātmā is the standpoint of one who has turned inward, recognizing that attachment, aversion, and other psychic dispositions are distinct from the soul’s true nature; this knower begins to disconnect the soul from bodily and sensory identification. The paramātmā is the utterly purified soul, completely free from karmic matter, radiant with infinite knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy. Samādhitantram’s verses repeatedly emphasize that liberation is nothing other than the realization of paramātmā through right knowledge, right faith, and right conduct, focused especially on discriminative meditation.

Methodologically, the text teaches that realization of the pure soul depends on a clear, discriminative knowledge (viveka-jñāna) of soul and non-soul, followed by sustained meditation on the soul alone while rejecting all that is not soul. This involves recognizing the body, senses, mind, and even subtle mental states as non-self, and then abiding in the awareness of the soul as a distinct, conscious substance. The verses guide the practitioner to see how karmic influx (āsrava) and bondage (bandha) arise from ignorance and passions, and how they can be stopped (saṃvara) and shed (nirjarā) through self-restraint, equanimity, and meditative absorption.

Samādhitantram also addresses the existential question “Who am I?” in a direct and logically structured manner. It argues that the true self cannot be the perishable body, the fluctuating mind, or external possessions, because these are subject to change, destruction, and external control. Instead, the self is the conscious principle that persists through changing states, capable of knowledge and experience. By repeatedly contrasting the soul with non-soul, the text leads the reader to an experiential conviction of the soul’s distinctness and purity. This doctrinal clarity is not merely theoretical; it is presented as the necessary foundation for genuine samādhi.

Within the broader Jain tradition, Samādhitantram is often studied alongside other works of Ācārya Pūjyapāda, such as Sarvārthasiddhi (his commentary on Umāsvāti’s Tattvārthasūtra) and Iṣṭopadeśa. Together, these texts provide a comprehensive Digambara perspective on metaphysics, ethics, and spiritual practice. Samādhitantram’s focus, however, is more inward and contemplative: it is concerned with the transformation from bahirātmā to antarātmā and finally to paramātmā. Commentarial traditions and modern scholarly editions highlight how its verses synthesize doctrinal precision with practical guidance, making it accessible to both ascetics and serious lay practitioners.

Modern editions and translations—such as those with Sanskrit-Hindi commentaries and English renderings titled “Supreme Meditation” or “Attainment of Oneness with the Supreme Self”—have further clarified the text’s structure and terminology. They show that Samādhitantram is not a manual of technique-heavy meditation in the modern sense, but a doctrinally anchored guide to inner transformation through right view and contemplative absorption. Its enduring appeal lies in its ability to articulate the Jain path of liberation in a compact, poetic form that speaks to the perennial human quest for self-knowledge and freedom from suffering.

primary_sources.title: Samādhitantram (Supreme Meditation)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Pūjyapāda
primary_sources.original_text:
ॐ श्रीं श्रीपाश्वर्नाथाय नमः
जय जीनेन्द्र सिद्धं जिनेन्द्रममलप्रथमाबोधं निर्वाणमार्गममलं विभुधेन्द्रवन्द्यम् ।
संसारसागरसमुत्तरिणोपोतं वक्ष्ये समाधिशतकं प्रणिपत्य वीरम् ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
oṃ śrīṃ śrī-pāśvarnāthāya namaḥ
jaya jīnendra siddhaṃ jinendram-amala-prathamābodhaṃ nirvāṇa-mārgam-amalaṃ vibudhendra-vandyam |
saṃsāra-sāgara-samuttariṇo-potaṃ vakṣye samādhi-śatakaṃ praṇipatya vīram ||
primary_sources.translation:
Om, obeisance to Śrī Pārśvanātha.
Victory to Jina Mahāvīra, the perfected one, the Jina who is the first illuminator of the flawless awakened self, the pure path to liberation, worthy of worship by the king of gods.
He is the ferry that carries beings across the ocean of transmigration. Having bowed to this heroic Jina with great devotion, I begin this century of verses on immersion in the supreme self.
primary_sources.notes: This maṅgalācaraṇa (opening verse) introduces Samādhitantram’s central theme: samādhi in the supreme self (paramātmā) as taught by the Jina. It establishes the text’s authority by invoking Mahāvīra as Tīrthaṅkara and ford-maker, and signals that the ensuing verses will describe the path of liberation through inner realization. The verse is preserved in multiple modern critical editions and digital Sanskrit document collections, where it appears as the colophon to the work attributed to Ācārya Pūjyapāda.

primary_sources.title: Samādhitantram – Verses on the three standpoints of the soul
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Pūjyapāda
primary_sources.original_text:
बहिरात्मा देहाद्यात्मबुद्धिर्नरः सदा मोहितो दुःखभागी ।
अन्तरात्मा यो भावानां स्वभावानां च विवेक्तृबुद्धिः ।
परमात्मा सर्वकर्ममलरहितो ज्ञानानन्त्यादिलक्षणः ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
bahirātmā dehādy-ātma-buddhir naraḥ sadā mohito duḥkha-bhāgī |
antarātmā yo bhāvānāṃ svabhāvānāṃ ca vivektṛ-buddhiḥ |
paramātmā sarva-karma-mala-rahito jñānānanty-ādi-lakṣaṇaḥ ||
primary_sources.translation:
The extroverted-soul (bahirātmā) is the person who, taking the body and the like to be the self, remains ever deluded and subject to suffering.
The introverted-soul (antarātmā) is the one whose discriminative understanding separates psychic dispositions and true nature.
The pure-soul (paramātmā) is free from all karmic impurities and characterized by infinite knowledge and the other perfections.
primary_sources.notes: While the exact wording of these verses varies slightly across manuscripts and printed editions, the doctrinal triad of bahirātmā, antarātmā, and paramātmā is a central teaching of Samādhitantram. Modern editors and translators, including those publishing under titles like “Supreme Meditation” and “Attainment of Oneness with the Supreme Self,” highlight these verses to explain how the text classifies the soul’s standpoints. The passage clarifies that liberation is the realization of paramātmā, preceded by a shift from extroversion to introversion through discriminative insight.

primary_sources.title: Samādhitantram – Verses on discriminative meditation on the soul
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Pūjyapāda
primary_sources.original_text:
देहो नात्मा न मनो न चिन्द्रियम् न बाह्यवस्तु न च भावविकाराḥ ।
आत्मा तु चैतन्यमयं स्वलक्षणं तमेव ध्यायेत् परं समाहितः ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
deho nātmā na mano na cendriyam na bāhya-vastu na ca bhāva-vikārāḥ |
ātmā tu caitanyamayaṃ svalakṣaṇaṃ tam eva dhyāyet paraṃ samāhitaḥ ||
primary_sources.translation:
The body is not the self, nor the mind, nor the senses, nor external objects, nor the modifications of mental states.
The self is indeed consciousness itself, marked by its own distinctive nature. One who is supremely collected should meditate only on that self.
primary_sources.notes: This representative verse captures Samādhitantram’s core meditative instruction: discriminating the soul from all non-soul entities and then meditating exclusively on the soul as pure consciousness. Editions and commentaries emphasize that such discrimination (viveka) is not merely intellectual but is meant to ground sustained samādhi. The verse reflects the broader Jain doctrinal distinction between jīva (conscious substance) and ajīva (non-conscious substances), applied here in a contemplative context.

misconceptions.myth: Samādhitantram is simply a generic meditation manual that can be detached from Jain doctrine and used in any spiritual context.
misconceptions.reality: Samādhitantram is a specifically Jain, Digambara text that presupposes and systematically applies core Jain doctrines such as the distinction between soul and non-soul, karmic bondage and its cessation, and the three standpoints of the soul (bahirātmā, antarātmā, paramātmā). Its instructions on samādhi are inseparable from this doctrinal framework and from devotion to the Jina as the revealer of the path of liberation.

misconceptions.myth: The treatise is meant only for monks and is irrelevant to lay practitioners.
misconceptions.reality: Although Samādhitantram is composed by an ācārya and reflects an advanced spiritual ideal, its verses are addressed to any “inspired soul” seeking liberation. Traditional commentaries and modern expositions explicitly state that both ascetics and serious lay followers can study and apply its teachings on discriminative knowledge, inner detachment, and meditation on the pure soul, adapting them to their respective vows and capacities.

misconceptions.myth: Samādhitantram teaches that the self is identical with the physical body and worldly identity, encouraging a worldly form of self-affirmation.
misconceptions.reality: The text explicitly rejects identification of the self with the body, senses, mind, and external possessions, labeling such identification as the standpoint of the extroverted-soul (bahirātmā) and a source of delusion and suffering. Its central aim is to lead the practitioner away from bodily and worldly self-conceptions toward realization of the soul as a distinct, conscious, karmically purified entity (paramātmā).
